content.thinking:
I'm drafting the postmortem now, framing the root cause as demand saturation—traffic hit 4.5x against a fixed 3-core CPU cap at 3 replicas, with no deploys or flag changes involved. I should be careful to flag that the traffic surge's origin is unproven, the causal link is correlational rather than confirmed, and recovery after scale-out doesn't rule out the surge simply subsiding on its own.

I'm keeping the executive summary component-agnostic, referring to it as the "customer-facing shopping service" rather than naming internals, and I'll avoid stating precise error-rate figures since the ClientDisconnected errors look pre-existing and client-side rather than a genuine spike. For duration I'll just note roughly fourteen minutes since that's a required field, not an inferred metric.

I need to be upfront about the assumptions underlying this: the correlation between traffic and CPU wasn't experimentally isolated, the source of the traffic surge wasn't investigated, recovery was only briefly confirmed after scale-out (so it's possible the surge simply receded on its own), change history only covers about three hours prior so older changes aren't ruled out, the draft PR hasn't been reviewed or verified to fix anything, onset time came from automated detection, and I only looked at this service's own logs without checking upstream or downstream dependencies.

assumptions: The cause is correlational, not proven: traffic, CPU and latency moved together, but no test isolated CPU saturation as the mechanism.
Recovery is attributed to the scale-out, but the traffic surge could have receded at the same moment; the confirmation rested on roughly 44 seconds of observation after the action.
The origin of the traffic surge was never investigated - organic demand, a marketing event, a retry storm or bot traffic are all still open.
The change-event search covered only the ~3 hours before the incident, so an earlier deploy or config change is not ruled out.

The elevated errors were ClientDisconnected events that were already occurring at a similar rate before the onset, so they are assumed to be shoppers abandoning slow pages rather than server-side failures; this was not verified.
The 15:42 onset was placed automatically from metric inflection, not corroborated independently; the logs show the same error pattern before and after that point.
Only this service's own metrics and logs were examined - upstream callers and downstream dependencies were not checked directly.
The draft pull request has not been reviewed or merged, and there is no evidence yet that it addresses the capacity limit.
input.executive_summary: For about fourteen minutes on the afternoon of 27 September 2026 (15:42-15:56 UTC), the customer-facing shop service became slow. Shoppers loading account pages saw pages take noticeably longer to render, and a small additional share of requests failed - mostly shoppers giving up and closing the connection before the page finished. Nothing was released or reconfigured; the service simply received several times its normal traffic in a few minutes and had a fixed amount of computing capacity allocated to it, so once that capacity was fully used, requests began to queue. The automated on-call system picked up the alert, diagnosed the capacity shortfall, and added more capacity to the service; response times returned to normal within about a minute of the action, and a draft code change has since been proposed for engineers to review. No data was lost and no orders were known to be dropped.
input.root_cause: io-shop ran out of CPU headroom under a traffic surge: request volume climbed roughly 4.5x (about 1200 to 5400 req/min) in the ~10 minutes before the alert while cpu_used_cores rose in lockstep from ~0.75 to the fixed 3.0-core limit across 3 replicas, and p50/p95/p99 latency only began to balloon once CPU pinned at that ceiling. Memory was flat, no deploys, config changes or feature-flag changes were recorded in the hours beforehand, and no dependency was implicated, so the fault reads as demand outgrowing fixed capacity rather than a regression in the service itself; scaling the deployment out returned latency to baseline.
